case_study_insert.main_stem: Thorncliff Bay Resort (TBR) is a private limited company in the seaside hospitality and tourism sector on the south coast, employing a workforce of 90. Founded in 2011 by Priya Rathore, it operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership and sells 18,000 units a year, one unit being an occupied room-night at an average selling price of $160. TBR plans to invest $900,000 in a new sea-view wing and spa, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year and a variable cost of $60 a unit. TBR faces rising labour turnover among housekeeping staff and guest complaints about slow check-in at peak weekends.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Guest and Operations Report, Q4 2025: TBR recorded 4,500 room-nights last quarter with 14 online service complaints, down from 26 a year earlier. Average check-in time was 8.4 minutes against a 5-minute target, and the housekeeping defect rate (rooms failing inspection) was 3.6%, down from 5.1%. A survey of 750 guests found that 68% would pay up to $12 more for a sea-view spa room and 57% choose hotels on sustainability credentials. Staff records show 31 of 90 employees have not yet completed on-the-job training on the new check-in system; off-the-job training at the local hotel college costs $480 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Thorncliff Bay Resort as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Tourism Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.5%, increasing debt-service costs for TBR's variable-rate $600,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.2% from $14.07 to $14.80 an hour from April 2026, affecting housekeeping and front-of-house rosters. (3) Inbound tourist arrivals are forecast to grow 8.3%, while hotel energy and food input costs have risen 9.6% and domestic holiday inflation is 6.4%.

questions.question_text: TBR plans to fund part of its new sea-view wing and spa with a $600,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for TBR of using the $300,000 retained profit instead of borrowing more.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using the $300,000 retained profit avoids all interest and repayment charges on that portion of the $900,000 sea-view wing and spa, protecting TBR's cash flow at a time when it already carries fixed costs of $420,000 a year and faces a base-rate rise to 4.5%. Every dollar not paid to the lender can instead cover the 9.6% increase in hotel energy and food inputs or fund the new spa's launch, so the resort can hold its $160 selling price rather than passing costs to guests. Retained profit is also immediately available, with no loan-approval delay before the building work starts.

Point 2: Retained profit requires no collateral and no fixed monthly instalments, so Priya Rathore's resort is not exposed to repossession risk if the new wing attracts fewer bookings than forecast, which matters given the rising labour turnover among housekeeping staff. It also keeps ownership and control within the existing company: a larger loan would let the lender impose conditions on how the sea-view wing is run. Using the $300,000 first therefore reduces the $600,000 bank loan actually needed, cutting TBR's debt commitment while it tackles slow peak-weekend check-in and a 5.2% wage rise.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to TBR's wing investment, costs and borrowing.

questions.question_text: TBR is promoting its new sea-view wing and spa. Consider a national television campaign, regional radio advertising, and social media travel influencers. Which should TBR choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: A television advertisement would build awareness of the new sea-view wing and spa quickly across the south coast and beyond, reaching the 68% of surveyed guests who would pay $12 more for such a room and helping justify the $900,000 investment. However, airtime and production are expensive for a 90-employee resort already servicing a $600,000 bank loan, and much of the audience lives outside TBR's drive-to catchment, so a large share of the spend would be wasted.

Regional radio advertising: Local radio is far cheaper and can target drive-to weekend guests within the resort's catchment, with flexible short-notice messages about spa breaks. Its weakness is reach and format: radio cannot show the sea views or the refurbished spa, and it will not reach the corporate and tour guests who make up much of the 18,000 room-nights, so it is unlikely to fill a whole new wing on its own.

Social media travel influencers: Travel and wellness influencers can show the sea-view spa visually to exactly the segment identified in TBR's research — the 57% of 750 guests who choose hotels on sustainability credentials and the 68% willing to pay $12 more. Engagement is measurable, cost per reached guest is low, and user-generated content keeps promoting the wing after launch. Results build more slowly than television and depend on choosing credible influencers.

Recommendation: TBR should choose social media travel influencers, backed by modest local radio for last-minute weekend availability. Influencers give visual reach at a fraction of television's cost and directly target the guests whose stated preferences justify the $900,000 wing. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted while TBR carries a $600,000 loan and $420,000 fixed costs; radio alone is rejected because it cannot display the spa or reach enough guests to fill 18,000 room-nights. The $300,000 retained profit can fund the campaign without new debt.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to TBR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of TBR with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of TBR with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: TBR's labour turnover among housekeeping staff is rising and check-in complaints are high. Explain two benefits for TBR of using its democratic leadership style to address these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives TBR's workforce of 90 a genuine voice in how housekeeping and reception are organised, which addresses the rising labour turnover directly. When staff help design room-allocation rotas or suggest ways to cut the 8.4-minute check-in time towards the 5-minute target, they develop ownership and job satisfaction (Herzberg's motivators), so they are more likely to stay. Retaining experienced housekeepers protects service quality while the new sea-view wing opens and avoids the disruption of repeatedly recruiting and inducting replacements.

Point 2: Consulting the employees who actually clean rooms and greet guests generates practical improvements that management may miss. Housekeeping suggestions can target the weaker areas behind guest complaints and the 3.6% inspection defect rate, while reception ideas can smooth peak-weekend check-in, reducing the 14 complaints. Involvement also raises morale and attendance, easing pressure on the team when the minimum wage rises 5.2% to $14.80 and TBR must protect its $100 contribution per room-night. Democratic leadership suits a resort that needs fast, local problem-solving rather than purely top-down instructions.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to TBR's turnover, complaints and costs.

questions.question_text: TBR must train 31 staff on the new check-in system. Consider on-the-job training and off-the-job training at the local hotel college. Which should TBR choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching the 31 untrained staff at the front desk uses TBR's own check-in system and real guest situations, so learning is directly transferable and employees stay productive during peak weekends. It costs no course fees, which protects cash while the resort services a $600,000 loan, and trainers can correct the specific causes of the 8.4-minute check-in time immediately. The drawback is that trainers are themselves reception or housekeeping staff whose normal duties suffer, and bad habits can be passed on; with 14 complaints already recorded, inconsistent teaching could make service less reliable.

Off-the-job training: The local hotel college course at $480 per employee gives structured, up-to-date customer-service skills and a recognised certificate for all 31 staff. The full cost is 31 × $480 = $14,880, which is modest beside the $900,000 wing investment and can be met from the $300,000 retained profit. It also removes staff from the desk for several days, reducing capacity during busy periods, and generic course content may not match TBR's exact check-in software, so some on-site follow-up would still be needed after the course.

Decision: TBR should choose on-the-job training as the main method, backed by short college modules for senior receptionists. On-the-job training is cheaper, system-specific and keeps the desk staffed while complaints are reduced and labour turnover is high; full off-the-job training is rejected because losing 31 staff from the front desk at once would worsen the 8.4-minute check-in problem and add $14,880 for content that still needs on-site adaptation. College placements can be added for new recruits once the new wing opens.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to TBR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of TBR.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of TBR with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and system relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TBR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $420,000 ÷ ($160 − $60) = $420,000 ÷ $100 = 4,200 units. Answer: break-even output is 4,200 room-nights a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $160 − $60 = $100. Answer: contribution per unit is $100.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TBR's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 4,200-unit break-even output with actual output of 18,000 room-nights: TBR has a margin of safety of 18,000 − 4,200 = 13,800 units, showing the resort can absorb a downturn in bookings before it stops covering its $420,000 fixed costs.
2. Use contribution per unit of $100 to model pricing: a discount of $12 a room-night would leave $88 contribution, letting managers judge whether extra volume from the new spa still covers fixed costs and the $600,000 loan.
3. Set volume targets for servicing the $600,000 bank loan and for justifying the $900,000 sea-view wing: at $100 contribution each, 6,000 extra room-nights generate $600,000 of contribution.
4. Benchmark unit cost and labour productivity: average total cost is $420,000 ÷ 18,000 + $60 = $83.33 a room-night, and productivity is 18,000 ÷ 90 = 200 room-nights per employee, giving a baseline to track the impact of the 9.6% input-cost rise and of housekeeping turnover.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 4,200 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $100 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 13,800 units; pricing and discount modelling against $420,000 fixed costs; loan-service and investment volume targets for the $900,000 wing; and unit-cost benchmarking at $83.33 with labour productivity of 200 room-nights per employee.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TBR's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TBR's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.56 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.97 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.21 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $85,000 inventories + $120,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $240,000; 2025 current assets = $60,000 + $150,000 + $55,000 = $265,000. Coverage of short-term obligations 2024 = $240,000 ÷ $160,000 = 1.50; 2025 = $265,000 ÷ $170,000 = 1.56. Excluding stock: 2024 = ($240,000 − $85,000) ÷ $160,000 = $155,000 ÷ $160,000 = 0.97; 2025 = ($265,000 − $60,000) ÷ $170,000 = $205,000 ÷ $170,000 = 1.21.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures. Coverage of short-term obligations rose from 1.50 to 1.56 because current liabilities increased only from $160,000 to $170,000 while current assets grew by $25,000. More importantly, the stock-excluding measure jumped from 0.97 to 1.21, so TBR is no longer dependent on selling linen and food inventories to meet its short-term debts — valuable while it services a $600,000 bank loan and builds a $900,000 wing. The concern is trade receivables rising from $120,000 to $150,000; if corporate guests and tour operators pay late, cash could tighten quickly. Inventories fell to $60,000, so stock availability for peak weekends should be monitored.

Conclusion: TBR's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher in 2025 and the improvement does not rely on inventory, with the 0.97 to 1.21 move the clearest evidence of stronger underlying liquidity. TBR should tighten credit control on receivables before drawing further on finance for the spa.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TBR of responding to the 57% of surveyed guests who choose hotels on sustainability credentials.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Acting on the 57% of 750 guests who choose hotels on sustainability credentials, alongside the 68% who would pay $12 more for a sea-view spa room, lets TBR charge a premium that protects its $100 contribution per room-night even while hotel energy and food input costs rise 9.6%. A credible eco-refurbishment of the $900,000 sea-view wing also strengthens the resort's brand with eco-conscious travellers, helping win repeat bookings and defend the $160 selling price against inflation of 6.4%.

Disadvantage: Sustainable materials and spa amenities usually cost more than standard fittings, which could push the $60 variable cost per unit upward and squeeze the margin unless the full $12 premium is accepted by guests. The survey records stated preferences, not guaranteed bookings, so there is a risk that the extra spend in the new wing is not recovered through higher occupancy. TBR must also avoid vague green claims: if the sustainability message is not backed by real changes, the 57% segment may distrust it, and any rework would add to the $420,000 fixed costs at a time when labour turnover is already rising.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to TBR's survey data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 5.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in energy and food input costs will affect TBR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): If TBR's $600,000 bank loan tracks the base rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000). That is small against fixed costs of $420,000 and can be largely removed by fixing the loan rate. Higher borrowing costs would also raise the price of any future finance for the $900,000 wing, but the direct hit is modest.

Minimum wage increase (5.2%, to $14.80 an hour): Housekeeping and front-of-house roles at TBR are hourly paid, so this rise feeds into the wage bill and is not optional. The insert gives neither hours worked nor individual pay, so no annual total can be invented; the defensible judgement is qualitative against the given data of 200 room-nights per employee and $100 contribution per unit. If productivity holds, a wage rise is absorbable through the $12 room premium; if labour turnover disrupts service, unit labour costs rise and contribution is squeezed.

Energy and food input costs (9.6%): These apply to every one of the 18,000 room-nights. The insert does not decompose the $60 variable cost, so only a bound can be calculated honestly: if the whole variable cost rose 9.6%, that adds 9.6% × $60 = $5.76 a unit, or about $103,680 a year (18,000 × $5.76). Even a narrower increase would materially cut the $100 contribution that justifies the spa investment. TBR can recover part through the $12 premium and supplier renegotiation.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in energy and food inputs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 18,000 units and directly erodes the $100 contribution underpinning the $900,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise is small and fixable by fixing the loan rate, and the wage rise can be offset by productivity and the $12 premium. Input-cost inflation therefore deserves the most urgent management response.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to TBR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TBR's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of TBR with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
